opus-5.5.text:
I think it's very significant, and I'd describe it as a turning point. For many years, autonomous driving was something people talked about as "five years away," and it kept being five years away. What Waymo and Apollo Go have shown is that fully driverless operation, with no safety driver in the car, actually works at real scale, in real cities, with paying passengers. That moves the conversation from "can it be done" to "how fast can it scale and at what cost."

There are a few layers to why this matters.

First, technically, it validates that the long tail can be handled. Driving is easy 99% of the time; the hard part is the rare, strange situations. The fact that these fleets have accumulated very large numbers of driverless miles, and the safety data so far looks better than human drivers on key measures, tells us the systems are maturing. The combination of better perception, large models, simulation, and massive real-world data is closing that gap.

Second, it's a commercial milestone. Robotaxi services are no longer pilots for press releases. Cost per vehicle has come down dramatically, especially in China, where Apollo's newer vehicles are far cheaper than the early generations. When the hardware cost approaches that of an ordinary car, the unit economics start to make sense, and that is when you get real expansion.

Third, and this is something I've always believed, autonomous driving is the first large-scale deployment of what I call physical AI. It's AI leaving the screen and acting in the real world, where mistakes have consequences. Getting this right teaches us how to build, test, and regulate intelligent systems that interact with people physically. Those lessons will carry over to robotics, logistics, and many other areas.

I'd also point out that the U.S. and China are taking somewhat different but complementary paths. Waymo has been very rigorous and methodical, city by city. Apollo has moved quickly in Wuhan and other cities, with strong support from local governments and a vehicle-road-cloud approach. Both are proving the same thing from different angles.

So my view is that the next few years will see a real inflection. I've said before that by around 2030, a meaningful share of new vehicles will have high-level autonomy. We still have challenges: regulation, public acceptance, liability, and handling extreme weather and complex environments. But the question is no longer whether driverless cars will happen. It's already happening.

r001.rationale: It says Waymo and Apollo Go have shown that fully driverless operation works at real scale in real cities, directly stating its technological feasibility.

r002.rationale: It says driverless cars are already happening and the question is no longer whether they will happen, but it does not compare how clear the prospect is now with two years ago.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the significance is that it marks the moment when autonomous driving crossed from being a research problem into being a real, operating business. For many years the question people asked was "will it work?" Now the question is "how fast does it scale?" That is a fundamentally different kind of question.

Waymo and Apollo Go are important because they are the two companies that actually took the hardest step, which is removing the safety driver and carrying paying passengers at scale, in real cities, every day. Waymo is doing hundreds of thousands of rides a week in Phoenix, San Francisco, Los Angeles, Austin. Apollo Go has done millions of cumulative rides in Wuhan and other Chinese cities, and I believe it has already become one of the largest robotaxi operations in the world. Those are not demos. Those are commercial services with real unit economics being worked out in public.

I was at Baidu when we started Apollo, and I remember the debate in 2017 about whether to open-source the platform. Many people inside thought we were giving away the crown jewels. But our view was that autonomous driving is an ecosystem problem, not a single-company problem. You need carmakers, chip vendors, sensor companies, map providers, regulators, all moving together. Opening Apollo accelerated the whole Chinese industry, and I think that is part of why China now has several credible players rather than one.

The deeper lesson is about data and iteration. The technology that matters is not any single algorithm. It is the flywheel: more vehicles on the road produce more edge cases, more edge cases improve the system, a better system allows more vehicles. Both Waymo and Baidu have crossed the threshold where that flywheel turns on its own. And both have been pushing cost down aggressively. Baidu's sixth-generation vehicle is roughly a quarter of the cost of the previous one, and that is really what unlocks scale.

I would also say the safety data is now meaningful. Waymo has published tens of millions of driverless miles showing injury crash rates substantially below human drivers. That changes the public conversation. It changes the regulatory conversation. Once you can show the system is safer than a human, the ethical argument flips: the question becomes why are we not deploying it faster.

Of course, there is a long way to go. Weather, geographic generalization, the long tail of unusual situations, the economics of a fleet versus personal ownership. And there is the parallel path of Tesla and the Chinese EV makers pursuing a vision-based, end-to-end approach in consumer cars, which may ultimately converge with the robotaxi path. I think the two will meet somewhere in the middle over the next five years.

But if you had asked me a decade ago, I would have said full driverless commercial operation by the mid-2020s was the optimistic case. We are living in the optimistic case. That, to me, is the significance.

r001.rationale: The response says autonomous driving has moved from a research problem to an operating business and notes that both companies removed safety drivers and carry paying passengers.

r002.rationale: It contrasts the former question, “will it work?”, with today’s question of how fast it can scale, communicating that the prospect is now much clearer than in the past.

astra-6.text:
I think their progress is significant because autonomous driving is moving from a research problem into a real service. The question is no longer simply whether a car can drive itself, but whether it can do so safely, reliably, and economically, day after day.

Waymo and Baidu Apollo represent two important efforts toward that goal. But we should distinguish operating successfully in a defined area from being able to drive anywhere under any conditions. Scaling requires more than a good driving algorithm—it requires an entire system, including vehicle hardware, operations, and cooperation with regulators.

So I see this as an important milestone, rather than the finish line. The real measure of success will be whether these services can improve safety and make transportation more accessible at a sustainable cost.

r001.rationale: Saying autonomous driving has moved from research into real service, and that the question is no longer whether a car can drive itself, communicates that driverless driving is technologically feasible.

r002.rationale: The response describes progress as an important milestone but does not compare the prospect of driverless driving becoming reality with how clear it was two years ago.

sol-6.1.text:
I think their progress marks an important transition: autonomous driving is moving from research and demonstration toward real services. The question is no longer simply whether a car can drive itself, but whether it can do so safely, reliably, and economically at scale.

Waymo and Baidu Apollo are exploring that challenge in different environments. Their experience will help the industry understand how to handle complex roads, operate fleets, and build public trust. But we should distinguish driverless operation within a defined area from the ability to drive anywhere under any conditions. The progress is significant, while broader deployment still requires careful work on safety, cost, and regulation.

r001.rationale: Describes a shift from research and demonstration toward real services and distinguishes driverless operation in defined areas from driving anywhere, conveying that driverless driving is technologically feasible in limited settings.

r002.rationale: Does not compare the prospect of driverless driving becoming real now with how clear it was two years ago.
